title: Ambiguity exhibit
description: One case in which a dispute turned on genuine textual ambiguity in a written legal instrument. The schema is the editorial policy: a case that cannot fill these fields does not belong in the collection.

id.description: Stable slug. Never change it once published — it is the permalink.

title.description: The human hook, phrased as the question the court faced. 'Is a burrito a sandwich?' not 'White City v. PR Restaurants'.

jurisdiction.description: ISO-ish: US-federal, US-MA, UK, CA, AU, EU.

prior_history.description: Note reversals here — a case that flipped is worth more than one that did not.

drafted_by.description: Who wrote it. Records the cases where the drafter lost on their own words.

mechanism.description: The linguistic axis. Enforced as an enum so the collection cannot silently become twenty comma cases.

quote.description: VERBATIM. The words in dispute and just enough around them to parse. Never edit for readability.

locus.description: The exact span the ambiguity lives in, e.g. 'the comma before "unless and until"'.

languages.description: For multilingual instruments only: each equally authentic version, verbatim.

readings.description: The discrete parses. If you cannot write at least two, this is vagueness and the case does not belong here.

statement.description: The reading in plain words. A reader must be able to see why someone believed it.

court_declared_ambiguous.description: Did the court concede the text was ambiguous? FALSE is the interesting case: it makes the 'declared clear, and the world disagreed' wing a query rather than a curatorial opinion.

quote.description: REQUIRED VERBATIM, never a paraphrase. Adversarial review of an earlier draft killed four of five claims in this collection, and every one was a paraphrased characterisation of a court's reasoning. Quote the holding or do not make the claim.

stakes.description: Omit rather than guess. Stakes differ in KIND, not just amount — liberty is not a dollar figure.

amount.description: As documented, with currency. e.g. 'USD 3.5bn per occurrence'.

documented.description: False means the figure comes from reporting, not the opinion. Say so on the page.

inclusion_test.description: The criterion, made auditable. A reviewer can check these three booleans against the exhibit without re-reading the opinion.

discrete_readings.description: Test (a). Two or more enumerable parses.

boundary.description: Present only on exhibits that press against the collection's own rules. Five of the twelve do, which makes them central rather than marginal, so the case against each one is recorded as structured fields instead of being buried in prose. A reader should be able to disagree with the editors using the editors' own strongest counter-argument.

tests.description: Which exclusion or criterion this exhibit strains.

against_inclusion.description: The strongest argument that this exhibit does NOT qualify, stated as its best advocate would state it. Where a judge made the argument, quote or cite them. Weakening it here to make the inclusion look easier defeats the purpose.

why_included.description: Why the editors kept it anyway, answering the argument above directly.

notes.description: Optional further commentary. For boundary specimens the case for and against belongs in the boundary object, not here.

sources.description: Provenance per field, not per exhibit. A secondary source may support stakes; it may never be the sole support for citation, disputed_text, or the resolution quote.

kind.description: What the source IS, not how prestigious its host is. The test is whether the document reproduces the report or summarises it. primary = the court's own text as issued (a slip opinion, a court or government site); for cases predating law reporting as we know it there is no such artefact, and the nominate report is the record, so a faithful reprint of it counts as near-primary at worst. near-primary = a faithful reproduction of that text by anyone (CourtListener, BAILII, Justia, a scanned reprint hosted by a university). A course-page PDF that reproduces counsel's argument and the bench's interjections is worth more here than a polished publisher's page that prints only the headnote. secondary = commentary, journalism, case briefs, anything that paraphrases. May support stakes or background; may never be the sole support for a citation, the disputed text, or the resolution quote.

status.description: 'confirmed' requires the citation, the disputed text, and the resolution quote each backed by a primary or near-primary source. Nothing else publishes.

pairs_with.description: Exhibit ids that argue against or illuminate this one. The collection's best content is in the pairings, not the entries.

preventive_edits.description: The smallest textual change that forces EACH reading, not just the one the court picked. Recording only the edit that produces the litigated outcome quietly makes that outcome the drafting baseline, as though the losing party's reading were the error rather than the other half of a choice the drafter failed to make. Every reading gets an entry. What the exhibit then shows is that syntax encodes a decision, and that the drafter had to make it either way.

forces.description: The reading id this edit makes unavoidable.

edit.description: The smallest change that forecloses every other reading. Quote the revised wording where it is short enough to quote.

plausible_intent.description: Whether anyone could actually have WANTED this reading. A reading can be a plausible parse and an implausible intention: Chef America's winning construction incinerates the product, so it is draftable but nobody was ever going to draft it. False here is not a judgment that the court was wrong, only that the edit reconstructs an intention no party held.

changes_bargain.description: Where choosing this reading moves money, risk or entitlement rather than merely clarifying, say how. This is what stops the two edits reading as interchangeable when one of them doubles an insurer's limit.
